title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 3: Not Only Prosperity, But Also Peace
keywords: Not Only Prosperity, But Also Peace

primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's address to the Legal Management Council of the Philippines answering the criticism that the Supreme Court 'had been interfering unreasonably in economic governance,' and arguing that courts have decided commercial controversies for more than a century and cannot now be excluded from them.

A defense of judicial competence over economic questions: jurists 'may not be economists, but they must still decide cases arising from oil cartels, deregulation laws, and the privatization of government-run businesses,' because judges are expected to have 'a working idea of all branches of human knowledge, including economics.'

Six guidelines showing the Court has been 'prudent, transparent and careful' in economic cases -- deference to the political branches, avoidance of political questions, laissez-faire toward private contracts, respect for lower courts and specialized agencies, insistence on an actual 'case and controversy,' and extra vigilance over public contracts.

The constitutional duty not to evade: to 'cop out and refuse to decide controversial economic issues' would be dereliction, because the Constitution imposes on the judiciary 'the solemn duty, not just the power or authority, to settle all issues of grave abuse of discretion' -- the Court safeguards 'not only prosperity but also peace.'
sub_topics: He opens as a returning member -- a former vice-president and board member of the LMCP, the 'collegium' where the late Senator Rene 'Compañero' Cayetano 'developed his wings of leadership' -- and urges the corporate lawyers, who already have fame and fortune, to give 'time, talent and treasure' to government service.

He names the criticism directly: LMCP President Ariel F. Abonal's invitation asked how the Court decided cases involving the business community, a request he reads as prompted by 'unfounded criticisms' that the Court has no commercial expertise and should stay out of economic cases.

Courts have adjudicated commercial disputes for over a century -- suits under the Spanish-era Code of Commerce, sales and leases, construction, interest rates, natural-resource agreements -- and now face information-age and bioscientific questions like patents, genetically modified organisms, in vitro fertilization and cloning.

He poses the counter-question: if the judiciary were excluded from these disputes, 'who or what agency would then settle them? And by what laws and under what standards?' -- excluding economic issues 'would merely create new ones with no answers.'

Expertise is not the test: judges are not physicians or engineers or computer geeks either, yet decide murder, condominium and e-commerce cases; it is for the parties 'to educate the courts on the technical aspects of their cases.'

First guideline -- deference: as a rule the Court respects the branches with primary responsibility for economic development, as in Tañada v. Angara, where the Senate's ratification of the WTO treaty was 'presumed regular and done in good faith.'

Second guideline -- political questions: the Court does not review the wisdom of trade liberalization or globalization, matters the people gave the President and Congress; but a political question becomes justiciable where unconstitutionality or grave abuse of discretion is involved, the Court reviewing obedience to constitutional limits rather than wisdom.

Third guideline -- private transactions: a laissez-faire policy governs purely private commercial contracts, since 'neither the law nor the courts will extricate a party from an unwise or undesirable contract'; the notable exception is equity relief against 'excessive, iniquitous, unconscionable, and exorbitant' interest -- 10 percent compounded monthly, 66 percent, even 192 percent per annum.

Fourth guideline -- respect for other tribunals: decisions of the Court of Appeals, constitutional commissions and specialized agencies (NLRC, Monetary Board, ERC, SEC and others) are upheld absent 'reversible errors' or grave abuse, supported by the doctrines of primary jurisdiction and exhaustion of administrative remedies and by the presumption of regular official duty.

Fifth guideline -- the Court has not waived 'case and controversy': under Velarde v. SJS a petition must state what specific legal right was violated and by what acts, complaints must state a cause of action, and 'the rendering of advisory opinions is beyond the constitutional mandate of the judiciary.'

What may be waived: locus standi and the hierarchy of courts are set aside in controversies of transcendental importance, since parties with standing often benefit from void government contracts and would never sue, leaving them 'unassailed.'

Sixth guideline -- public contracts draw extra vigilance, illustrated by four voided agreements: Chavez v. PEA (Amari's reclaimed and submerged Manila Bay land), Agan v. Piatco (NAIA Terminal III, monopoly and the 'fair competition essence'), Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec (automated counting machines and 'leveling the playing field'), and Jaworski v. PAGCOR (delegated online gambling franchise).

Two refinements: in MMDA v. Jancom a contract was valid and perfected yet ineffective until signed by the President under its own Article 19; and in JG Summit the Court reversed itself on reconsideration, ruling a shipyard was NOT a public utility and upholding Kawasaki's right to own more than forty percent of Philippine Shipyard and Engineering Corporation.

He closes by assuring the corporate bar that the Court knows 'integrity, stability and predictability' in decisions are needed for prosperity and shares policymakers' desire to attract investment -- but that its sworn duty to uphold the Constitution is 'its primary contribution to good governance.'

stances.claim: Excluding economic and commercial controversies from judicial review would solve nothing and would leave no one to protect the parties and the public 'from economic tyrannies, excesses and abuses.'
stances.rhetorical_move: rhetorical questions -- asking who else would decide, under what law and what standards

stances.claim: Lack of technical expertise is no bar to adjudication, because judges are expected to have a working idea of all branches of human knowledge and the parties can educate the court on the technical aspects of their cases.
stances.rhetorical_move: analogy -- judges are not physicians, engineers or computer geeks either, yet decide murder, construction and e-commerce cases

stances.claim: In deciding economic controversies the Supreme Court has been prudent, transparent and careful, deferring to the political branches, to lower courts and to specialized agencies, and intervening mainly where public funds and public contracts are involved.
stances.rhetorical_move: numbered guidelines, each anchored to a decided case

stances.claim: For justices to refuse controversial economic questions in order to stay in their comfort zones would be dereliction, because the Constitution imposes a duty -- not a mere power -- to settle all issues of grave abuse of discretion.
stances.rhetorical_move: duty-over-comfort contrast: naming the easier path and rejecting it

notable_anecdotes: He returns to the LMCP as an alumnus, recalling that before his appointment to the Supreme Court he was its vice-president and board member and that his colleagues there 'helped me hone myself for eventual service in the judiciary.'
He remembers the late Senator Rene 'Compañero' Cayetano as an LMCP contemporary who 'developed his wings of leadership' in the same association.
He quotes the invitation letter of LMCP President Ariel F. Abonal asking how the Court decided cases involving the business community, and reads it as a polite version of a standing criticism.
He cites the interest rates the Court has struck down as equity cases -- 10 percent compounded monthly, 66 percent per annum, and 'very recently, 192 percent per annum.'

He recounts the Court reversing itself in JG Summit, where a unanimous First Division ruling that a shipyard was a public utility was undone on reconsideration, allowing a Japanese company to own more than forty percent of a Subic Bay shipbuilder.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' collects CJP's address to the Legal Management Council of the Philippines, the association of corporate lawyers in which he had served as vice-president and board member before joining the Supreme Court and in which the late Senator Rene 'Compañero' Cayetano had 'developed his wings of leadership.' Taking up LMCP President Ariel F. Abonal's request to explain how the Court decided cases involving the business community, he answered the criticism that the Court had been interfering unreasonably in economic governance and lacked commercial expertise. He replied that courts had heard commercial disputes since the Spanish Code of Commerce, more than a century, and now faced patents, genetically modified organisms, in vitro fertilization and cloning; if the judiciary were excluded, he asked, who would settle such disputes, by what laws and under what standards, and who would protect the public from economic tyrannies and abuses. Expertise was no obstacle, since judges also decided murder, construction and e-commerce cases and were expected to have a working idea of all branches of human knowledge, with the parties educating the court on technical matters. He then set out six guidelines: deference to the political branches, as in Tañada v. Angara; abstention from political questions unless unconstitutionality or grave abuse of discretion appeared; a laissez-faire policy toward private contracts, excepting equitable relief from excessive, iniquitous, unconscionable and exorbitant interest; respect for the Court of Appeals, the constitutional commissions and specialized agencies; insistence on an actual case and controversy under Velarde v. SJS, though locus standi and the hierarchy of courts could yield to transcendental importance; and extra vigilance over public contracts, illustrated by Chavez v. PEA, Agan v. Piatco, the Comelec automation case and Jaworski v. PAGCOR, with MMDA v. Jancom and JG Summit as refinements. To cop out of such cases, he concluded, would be dereliction of the Court's sworn duty, which safeguards not only prosperity but also peace.
